hero.headline: Five killed, dozens injured in I-95 bus crash in Virginia
hero.body:
A bus collided with multiple vehicles on Interstate 95 in Stafford County, Virginia, resulting in five deaths and 34 injuries, according to state police.

The crash occurred on the southbound lanes of I-95, prompting authorities to shut down the highway while emergency crews responded. Among those killed were a 13-year-old and a 7-year-old child. State police have identified all five victims, though their names were not disclosed in initial reports.

The injured were transported to hospitals throughout the region for treatment. The exact severity of their injuries has not been publicly detailed by authorities.

The collision involved a bus striking several passenger vehicles. Investigators are still working to determine what caused the bus to hit the other cars on the roadway. At this time, officials have not indicated whether weather conditions, road hazards, or other factors contributed to the crash.

Stafford County is located approximately 50 miles south of Washington, D.C., along Interstate 95, one of the most heavily traveled corridors on the East Coast. The highway serves as a major transportation route connecting cities from Florida to Maine, with thousands of vehicles traveling through the area daily.

The investigation into the crash remains ongoing as authorities seek to understand the full circumstances of the collision. Police have not yet released information about the bus operator, whether the vehicle was part of a commercial service or privately operated, or its origin and intended destination at the time of the incident.

Emergency responders faced a challenging situation as they worked to assist the injured and secure the scene. The closure of southbound I-95 affected traffic flow through this busy corridor as investigators collected evidence and documented the scene.

This crash highlights the dangers on one of America's busiest highways, where high traffic volume and speed create hazardous conditions. The deaths of the two children have added to the tragedy of the incident, affecting families and communities in the region.

State police continue to appeal for any witnesses or information that might help investigators understand how the collision occurred. The incident serves as a reminder of how quickly serious accidents can happen on interstate highways, even in broad daylight or normal conditions.

The investigation will likely take several days or weeks to complete as authorities examine vehicle damage, roadway conditions, and other evidence. Once their work is finished, police will provide a more detailed account of what led to the crash and whether any citations or charges will be filed.

cards.headline: Trump to decide soon on Iran nuclear deal framework
cards.teaser: President Trump said he will soon make a decision on a tentative agreement with Iran after U.S. and Iranian negotiators reached a framework to extend a ceasefire and begin new nuclear talks.
cards.body:
President Trump met with advisers regarding a proposed framework agreement with Iran. U.S. and Iranian negotiators have agreed on the outline of a deal that would extend a ceasefire and restart nuclear negotiations, pending approval from both Trump and Iran's leadership.

Trump stated that opening the Strait of Hormuz must be part of any final agreement. Vice President Vance indicated the two sides have made progress in talks, describing them as "very close" to a complete deal.

cards.headline: Oil Prices Drop as U.S. and Iran Move Closer to Cease-Fire Extension
cards.body:
Oil prices fell as investors responded to signs that the United States and Iran were nearing an agreement to extend a cease-fire. Stock markets fluctuated throughout trading as market participants evaluated the tentative progress toward a pact.

The potential agreement between the two nations has introduced uncertainty into energy markets, where traders are adjusting positions based on the prospect of reduced tensions in the Middle East. Oil prices have been sensitive to developments in U.S.-Iran relations due to Iran's role as a major oil producer and the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz to global energy shipments.

Investors weighed the implications of an extended cease-fire, which could affect oil supply dynamics and regional stability. The negotiations have been closely watched by financial markets, with price movements reflecting changing assessments of the likelihood of a deal.

Stock markets showed mixed performance as traders processed the news. The uncertainty surrounding the final terms of any agreement and its duration contributed to volatility across major indices. Energy sector stocks moved in response to the changing oil price outlook.

The discussions between U.S. and Iranian officials represent an effort to maintain a temporary halt in hostilities. The cease-fire extension under consideration would build on an existing arrangement, though specific details of the proposed terms have not been made public.

Market analysts have noted that oil prices remain subject to rapid changes based on diplomatic developments. The current price decline reflects trader expectations that an agreement would reduce the risk of supply disruptions from the region. However, the preliminary nature of the talks has left room for continued price swings.

The negotiations come at a time when global oil markets have already experienced significant pressure. Crude oil is heading toward its largest monthly decline since 2020, according to market data. The combination of diplomatic progress and existing downward price trends has intensified the focus on energy sector performance as the month draws to a close.

cards.headline: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Preparing for Major Russian Attacks
cards.teaser: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine is bracing for large-scale attacks by Russia in the next 24 hours.
cards.body:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy warned that Russia is preparing significant military strikes against Ukraine within the next 24 hours. He called on the country to brace for major attacks as Russian offensive operations continue.

The warning underscores escalating tensions in the region. A Russian drone used in an overnight attack on Ukraine recently crashed into an apartment building in eastern Romania, injuring two people, according to Romanian authorities.

cards.headline: UN Adds Israeli and Russian Forces to Sexual Violence Blacklist
cards.teaser: The United Nations placed Israel and Russia on its list of countries and groups credibly suspected of patterns of rape and sexual violence in conflict zones.
cards.body:
The UN has added Israel and Russia to its blacklist for sexual violence in conflict zones, citing abuse by their security forces. The organization verified sexual abuse of 31 Palestinian men, women and children from Gaza and the occupied West Bank between 2023 and 2025, including cases of repeated gang rape and sexual violence used as torture.

Israel denied the accusations and condemned the report. This marks the first time Israel has been placed on the UN's sexual violence in warzones blacklist. The report listed dozens of countries and nonstate groups as credibly suspected of patterns of rape and sexual violence.

cards.headline: Authorities dismantle botnet controlling over 17 million devices
cards.teaser: Law enforcement took down a massive botnet linked to a Russia-based residential proxy network.
cards.body:
Authorities dismantled a botnet that had infected more than 17 million devices worldwide. The operation targeted what officials described as one of the largest known botnets in recent years.

The botnet was tied to a residential proxy network based in Russia. Residential proxy networks use compromised home internet connections to route traffic, making malicious activity harder to trace. The takedown involved coordination among multiple law enforcement agencies.

hero.headline: Russian Drone Hits Apartment Building in Romania
hero.body:
A Russian drone struck an apartment building in Galati, Romania, during an overnight attack on neighboring Ukraine, according to Romanian authorities. The incident injured two people and sparked a fire that forced the evacuation of several residents from the building.

Romania is a NATO member state, and the strike has triggered swift condemnation from the alliance and the European Union. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the alliance is "ready to defend every inch" of its territory following the incident. "Russia's reckless behaviour is a danger to us all," Rutte wrote on social media after speaking with Romanian President Nicusor Dan.

Romanian officials said the drone was likely hit over Ukraine by air defenses, which altered its flight path before it crashed into the residential building. The impact destroyed the roof and sparked a fire at the scene. Emergency services responded and the military scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and a helicopter.

The Romanian government convened an emergency meeting of its supreme council of national defense and summoned Russia's ambassador to the foreign ministry. Romania's foreign minister, Oana Toiu, said the country would formally communicate the consequences of the incident for diplomatic relations between Romania and Russia. She also indicated that Romania would discuss new sanctions packages at the European level.

The Romanian foreign ministry described the incident as a "grave and irresponsible escalation" and a serious breach of international law. It asked NATO to accelerate the transfer of anti-drone capabilities to Romania and suggested it would invoke Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which triggers formal discussions about threats to member states' security.

Vladimir Putin claimed without evidence that the drone might have been a stray Ukrainian weapon. He suggested that drone wreckage should be handed over to Russia for an independent investigation.

The European Commission President Ursula von der Leider said Russia's "war of aggression has crossed yet another line" and expressed solidarity with Romania. France's foreign minister also condemned the incident as irresponsible.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident demonstrated that Russian aggression poses a threat to all of Europe. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been pressing the United States to provide additional Patriot air defense missiles to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

The strike represents the latest instance of the Ukraine conflict extending beyond Ukraine's borders. Galati is located on the Danube River in eastern Romania, west of the borders with Moldova and Ukraine. The incident adds to growing concerns about Russia's broader campaign of hybrid warfare across Europe.

cards.headline: Kenya Arrests 8 Students After Fire Kills 16 at School Dormitory
cards.teaser: Kenyan authorities arrested eight students following a fire at a police-run school dormitory that killed 16 people.
cards.body:
A fire swept through a dormitory at Utumishi girls academy in Gilgil, Nakuru county, killing at least 16 students. The blaze erupted just after midnight at the school located about 76 miles northwest of Nairobi.

Kenyan authorities arrested eight students in connection with the fire. The education minister indicated the students could face charges the following week.

cards.headline: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Preparing for Major Russian Attacks
cards.teaser: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine is bracing for large-scale attacks by Russia in the next 24 hours.
cards.body:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy warned that Russia is preparing significant military strikes against Ukraine within the next 24 hours. He called on the country to brace for major attacks as Russian offensive operations continue.

The warning underscores escalating tensions in the region. A Russian drone used in an overnight attack on Ukraine recently crashed into an apartment building in eastern Romania, injuring two people, according to Romanian authorities.

cards.headline: Divers Rescue First Person Trapped in Flooded Laos Cave
cards.teaser: Rescue teams evacuated the first of five villagers found trapped in a flooded cave in Laos, with two others still missing.
cards.body:
An international rescue team has successfully extracted the first survivor from a flooded cave in Xaysomboun province, central Laos. The man is now safe after divers navigated through narrow, water-filled tunnels filled with sharp rocks and collapse hazards to reach him.

Seven men entered the cave more than a week ago to hunt wildlife and search for gold before heavy rain blocked the entrance. Four survivors remain trapped in a chamber approximately 300 metres from the cave entrance, while two others have yet to be found. The rescue operation involves experienced divers, including some who participated in the 2018 Thai football team cave rescue.

cards.headline: Ghana Parliament Approves Bill Criminalizing LGBTQ Promotion
cards.teaser: Ghana's parliament passed legislation that criminalizes LGBTQ people and activity, according to an official statement.
cards.body:
Ghanaian lawmakers approved a bill that criminalizes the promotion of LGBTQ issues. The legislation would jail people who engage in same-sex activity for up to three years.

The parliament passed the new anti-LGBTQ bill despite opposition from minority lawmakers, who rejected proposed amendments. One official insisted that no anti-LGBTQ bill was presented to Ghana's president, though parliament confirmed passage of the legislation.

cards.headline: Ukrainian Experts Say Russian Oreshnik Missile Was Nine Years Old
cards.teaser: Ukraine reported that a Russian Oreshnik missile fired in January was nine years old and contained Belarusian components, contradicting Russian claims about the weapon.
cards.body:
Ukrainian experts examined parts of the Oreshnik missile and determined it was nine years old. Ukraine said the missile is not cutting-edge technology as Russia has claimed.

The missile contained components from Belarus, according to Ukrainian analysis. American specialists are studying wreckage from an Oreshnik missile that struck Ukraine. The weapon used kinetic penetrators as its payload.

cards.headline: Judge orders Trump's name removed from Kennedy Center
cards.teaser: A federal judge ruled that President Trump's name must be removed from the Kennedy Center and blocked the arts complex from closing for renovations.
cards.body:
A federal judge has ordered the removal of Donald Trump's name from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, DC. US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the venue cannot be renamed without an act of Congress, as it was clearly designated for the late President John F. Kennedy. The judge directed the Trump administration to remove all physical signage bearing Trump's name and eliminate references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials within 14 days.

The ruling also blocked the Kennedy Center from closing for planned renovations, at least temporarily. The decision preserves the center's current operations while the legal dispute continues.

cards.headline: Trump to decide soon on Iran nuclear deal framework
cards.teaser: President Trump said he will soon make a decision on a tentative agreement with Iran after U.S. and Iranian negotiators reached a framework to extend a ceasefire and begin new nuclear talks.
cards.body:
President Trump met with advisers regarding a proposed framework agreement with Iran. U.S. and Iranian negotiators have agreed on the outline of a deal that would extend a ceasefire and restart nuclear negotiations, pending approval from both Trump and Iran's leadership.

cards.headline: Kenyan court blocks U.S. Ebola quarantine facility plan
cards.teaser: A court in Kenya suspended a U.S. plan to establish a quarantine facility for American Ebola patients in the country.
cards.body:
A Kenyan court issued an order blocking the United States from proceeding with plans to build a quarantine facility for Americans who contract Ebola. The proposed facility would have kept U.S. citizens infected with the virus in Africa rather than transporting them to the United States for treatment.

U.S. officials said Americans who get Ebola will now go to Europe for treatment instead of to the United States. The proposal has drawn backlash both in Kenya and in the United States. The court suspension halts the plan while legal challenges proceed.

cards.headline: Former Des Moines school superintendent sentenced for citizenship fraud
cards.teaser: Ian Roberts, the former head of Des Moines schools, was sentenced to two years in prison for falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen.
cards.body:
Ian Roberts, the former superintendent of Des Moines schools, was sentenced to two years in prison for misrepresenting his U.S. citizenship status. He falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen when applying for and taking the leadership position at the Iowa school district.

Prosecutors presented documentation showing that Roberts submitted false statements about his citizenship during his employment. He is expected to face deportation following the completion of his prison sentence.

cards.headline: California governor polls show possible two-Democrat runoff
cards.teaser: New polling shows a growing chance that two Democrats could advance in California's gubernatorial race to replace outgoing Governor Newsom.
cards.body:
A second poll indicates the Becerra candidates are leading in California's race for governor. The latest surveys show a slim but increasing possibility that two Democrats could advance to the general election under the state's top-two primary system.

California's gubernatorial race to replace Newsom has drawn a crowded field of candidates. Polling suggests Democratic voters are showing limited enthusiasm for their choices in the contest. The top-two primary system allows the two highest vote-getters to advance regardless of party affiliation.

cards.headline: 18-year-old Fonseca defeats Djokovic at French Open
cards.teaser: Teenager Joao Fonseca upset Novak Djokovic in a five-set match in the third round of the French Open.
cards.body:
Brazilian teenager João Fonseca pulled off a career-defining upset against Novak Djokovic in a grueling five-set battle at the French Open third round. After Djokovic stormed to a two-set lead, the 19-year-old refused to surrender, mounting a remarkable comeback to win 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5, 7-5 after nearly five hours of play.

The match tested Djokovic's legendary resilience as the 39-year-old champion's body struggled against the younger opponent's relentless performance. Despite Djokovic's reputation for finding victory from difficult positions, Fonseca's courageous and headstrong tennis proved decisive. The loss extends Djokovic's wait for a record 25th Grand Slam singles title.

cards.headline: Blue Origin Rocket Explodes During Test at Cape Canaveral Launchpad
cards.teaser: Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket exploded during a test at its Florida launch facility, causing significant damage.
cards.body:
A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded during a scheduled hotfire test at Cape Canaveral's Kennedy Space Center on Thursday night at 9pm ET. The massive fireball destroyed the launchpad, and the blast was visible from miles away, with an orange sky reported as far south as Fort Pierce, 115 miles away.

No personnel were harmed in the incident, according to Blue Origin, which described the explosion as an anomaly. The explosion threatens NASA's lunar program, which depends partly on Blue Origin's launch capabilities for plans to build a lunar base and return humans to the moon within the next two years.

cards.headline: Universal Music Rejects Bill Ackman's $64 Billion Takeover Offer
cards.teaser: Universal Music Group turned down a buyout proposal from billionaire investor Bill Ackman's Pershing Square.
cards.body:
Universal Music Group rejected a takeover bid from Bill Ackman's investment firm Pershing Square, stating the offer fundamentally and materially undervalued the company. The proposal valued the music giant at approximately $64 billion to $65 billion.

Ackman, who is already a shareholder in Universal Music Group, made the buyout proposal through his Pershing Square investment vehicle. The company's board concluded that the bid did not reflect the true worth of the business. Universal Music Group is one of the largest music companies globally, representing major recording artists and controlling extensive music catalogs.

cards.headline: UnitedHealthcare Eliminates Prior Approval for Most Pediatric Services
cards.teaser: The health insurer will remove insurance approval requirements for nearly two-thirds of pediatric services.
cards.body:
UnitedHealthcare announced it will eliminate prior authorization requirements for a majority of pediatric medical services. The change affects nearly two-thirds of services that previously required advance insurance approval before treatment could proceed.

The policy shift means families and healthcare providers will no longer need to obtain permission from the insurance company before receiving or providing many types of care for children. Prior authorization has been a point of contention in healthcare, with medical providers arguing that the requirement delays necessary treatment and creates administrative burdens.

cards.headline: NextEra Energy's Political Influence in Florida Examined Amid Dominion Acquisition
cards.teaser: The utility company's use of political power in its home state faces scrutiny as it pursues a major acquisition.
cards.body:
NextEra Energy has frequently clashed with consumer groups, residents, and journalists in Florida while wielding considerable political power in the state. The utility company is currently pursuing an acquisition of Dominion Energy, representing a significant consolidation in the sector.

The scrutiny of NextEra's political activities intensifies as the company seeks to expand through the Dominion purchase. These disputes highlight broader concerns about the company's influence and operations in its home state during this pivotal expansion effort.

cards.headline: Wall Street Investors Anxious About Missing SpaceX Public Offering
cards.teaser: Elon Musk and bankers are working to convince investors that passing on the massive IPO carries greater risk than buying in.
cards.body:
Elon Musk and his banking team are creating momentum for a large SpaceX public offering by emphasizing the risks of not participating. The strategy aims to make investors feel that missing the opportunity presents a greater danger than the risks associated with purchasing shares.

The approach represents an effort to build demand for what would be a massive stock market debut. Wall Street firms are concerned about being left out of what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in recent years. The campaign seeks to generate a self-fulfilling prophecy of strong demand for SpaceX shares when they become available to public investors.

cards.headline: Providence Capitalizes on World Cup Proximity Despite Not Being Official Host
cards.teaser: Rhode Island officials are promoting their city to soccer fans due to its location near a World Cup stadium.
cards.body:
Providence, Rhode Island is leveraging its geographic advantage to attract World Cup visitors. A stadium outside Boston that will host seven World Cup matches is actually closer to Providence than to Boston itself, creating an unexpected opportunity for the city.

Rhode Island officials have recognized this strategic positioning and are working to draw fans to Providence during the tournament. The proximity puts the state in position to benefit from the influx of World Cup visitors without being designated as an official host city.

hero.headline: Justice Department sues states over rejected ICE undercover license plate requests
hero.body:
The Justice Department filed lawsuits against multiple states that refused to issue undercover license plates for Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicles. The legal action targets states that declined ICE requests for license plates that would allow agents to operate vehicles without obvious government identification.

The DOJ complaint centers on states that rejected the requests, which ICE says are necessary for enforcement operations. The agency has sought these plates to conduct surveillance and enforcement activities without vehicles being easily identified as government property.

The Justice Department has repeatedly accused websites that track ICE movements of doxing federal agents, but available evidence supporting these claims remains limited. The lawsuit represents an escalation in ongoing tensions between federal immigration enforcement and state governments over cooperation with ICE activities.

The undercover plates would allow ICE vehicles to blend in with civilian traffic during operations. States that refused the requests have not publicly detailed their reasons for the denials, and the Justice Department has not disclosed which specific states face lawsuits.

The legal dispute adds another dimension to broader conflicts between federal immigration authorities and state governments over enforcement priorities and cooperation. ICE has maintained that the specialized plates are standard law enforcement tools used by various federal agencies for covert operations.

The Justice Department's decision to pursue litigation suggests the administration views the license plate issue as significant to immigration enforcement capabilities. The cases will likely test the extent to which states must accommodate federal law enforcement equipment requests, particularly for immigration enforcement purposes.

Legal experts note the suits raise questions about state sovereignty and federal authority. The outcome could establish precedent for how states respond to similar federal requests for law enforcement support. The timeline for the cases and which courts will hear them has not been announced.

cards.headline: Authorities dismantle botnet controlling over 17 million devices
cards.teaser: Law enforcement took down a massive botnet linked to a Russia-based residential proxy network.
cards.body:
Authorities dismantled a botnet that had infected more than 17 million devices worldwide. The operation targeted what officials described as one of the largest known botnets in recent years.

The botnet was tied to a residential proxy network based in Russia. Residential proxy networks use compromised home internet connections to route traffic, making malicious activity harder to trace. The takedown involved coordination among multiple law enforcement agencies.

cards.headline: Texas measles outbreak data reveals high hospitalization rate
cards.teaser: About one in five measles cases required hospitalization, with most developing complications.
cards.body:
An analysis of a measles outbreak in Texas showed approximately 20 percent of patients required hospitalization. Most of those hospitalized developed complications from the virus.

The outbreak data underscores the medical risks posed by measles, a highly contagious disease preventable through vaccination. The hospitalization rate and complication frequency demonstrate the virus can cause severe illness requiring medical intervention.

cards.headline: FCC warns broadcasters to comply with directives after ABC settlement
cards.teaser: The Federal Communications Commission told all broadcasters to follow orders or face consequences similar to ABC.
cards.body:
The FCC issued a warning to broadcasters that they must comply with agency directives or face punishment similar to what ABC received. The warning followed ABC's recent settlement with the commission.

ABC stated that early license renewal for all of its stations was unprecedented and served no legitimate purpose. The network's comment suggests the settlement terms included unusual conditions not typically applied during standard license renewal processes.

cards.headline: Microsoft faces criticism for threatening security researcher with criminal probe
cards.teaser: A dispute between Microsoft and a security researcher reignited debate over software security responsibility.
cards.body:
Microsoft drew criticism after threatening a security researcher with criminal investigation over the disclosure of security vulnerabilities in its products. The company's legal response condemned what it characterized as uncoordinated vulnerability disclosure.

The public dispute has reignited long-standing debate about responsibility for software security. The researcher was subsequently removed from both GitHub and GitLab platforms following the conflict.

cards.headline: AI chip startup Groq seeks $650 million in funding after Nvidia deal
cards.teaser: Groq is raising funds as it shifts focus from hardware to AI inference technology.
cards.body:
Groq is raising $650 million in internal funding as it shifts away from hardware manufacturing. The chipmaker is redirecting its focus toward AI inference—the process that determines how AI models respond to user requests and prompts.

This strategic pivot positions Groq to compete in the expanding market for AI inference technology, which has become increasingly important as companies seek to improve the speed and quality of AI responses.

cards.headline: Companies replacing workers with AI face criticism over decision-making
cards.teaser: Box founder warns that executives deploying AI often lack understanding of affected jobs.
cards.body:
Executives making decisions to replace employees with AI often lack understanding of the actual work involved, according to Box founder Aaron Levie, who termed this pattern "AI psychosis." ClickUp recently cut 22 percent of its workforce in favor of AI agents, exemplifying broader trends in tech layoffs.

A TUC-backed report from the Institute for Public Policy Research calls for greater worker influence over AI adoption in the workplace. The thinktank argues employees need stronger bargaining power to ensure they share in AI's benefits, describing the current moment as pivotal for the future of work.

hero.headline: Indiana quarterback placed at least 40 bets on Hoosiers games
hero.body:
Brendan Sorsby placed at least 40 bets involving Indiana football while serving as a quarterback for the Hoosiers, according to court documents filed Friday. The filings reveal Sorsby used sportsbook accounts registered to a family member and friends to place the wagers.

Over four years, Sorsby wagered approximately $90,000 through these accounts. The court documents provide the first detailed accounting of the betting activity that led to his involvement in the ongoing investigation into sports gambling by college athletes.

The use of accounts registered to others allowed Sorsby to circumvent restrictions that prohibit college athletes from betting on sports in which they participate. The practice of using third-party accounts has emerged as a common pattern in recent investigations into athlete gambling violations across college sports.

Sorsby played quarterback for Indiana during the period covered by the betting activity detailed in the court filings. The documents do not specify whether the bets were placed on games in which Sorsby played or whether any of the wagers influenced game outcomes.

The revelation comes as multiple universities and athletic conferences have increased scrutiny of athlete gambling following several high-profile cases. College athletes are prohibited from betting on any sport sponsored by their institution, regardless of whether they participate in that sport.

The $90,000 total represents a substantial amount of wagering activity over the four-year period. The court documents filed Friday mark the first public disclosure of the specific number of bets and total amount wagered in Sorsby's case.

The filing does not indicate what charges Sorsby may face or whether other individuals involved in providing account access are under investigation. Indiana University has not publicly commented on the matter since the court documents were filed.

cards.headline: Djokovic loses in French Open third round
cards.teaser: Novak Djokovic's bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title ended with a third-round defeat to Joao Fonseca.
cards.body:
Novak Djokovic's bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title ended in the French Open third round on Friday, when 19-year-old Brazilian João Fonseca staged a stunning five-set comeback. After Djokovic won the first two sets 6-4, 6-4 on Court Philippe-Chatrier, Fonseca fought back to claim victory 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5, 7-5 in a marathon match lasting nearly five hours.

The 39-year-old Djokovic, struggling physically in the latter stages, was unable to close out the match despite his experience in such situations. Fonseca's courageous performance secured a career-defining win and advanced him to the fourth round of the tournament.

cards.headline: Magic finalizing deal to hire Spurs assistant as head coach
cards.teaser: The Orlando Magic are close to hiring San Antonio Spurs associate head coach Sean Sweeney as their new head coach.
cards.body:
The Orlando Magic are finalizing a deal to hire San Antonio Spurs associate head coach Sean Sweeney as their new head coach, according to ESPN sources on Friday.

Sweeney has served as an associate head coach under Gregg Popovich with the Spurs organization.

cards.headline: Steelers fire assistant coach for policy violation
cards.teaser: The Pittsburgh Steelers fired senior special teams assistant Derius Swinton II for violating club policy.
cards.body:
The Pittsburgh Steelers have fired senior special teams assistant Derius Swinton II due to a violation of club policy, according to ESPN sources. The dismissal was announced Friday.

The specific nature of the policy violation was not disclosed by the team.

cards.headline: Brewers reliever suspended one game for dugout incident
cards.teaser: Milwaukee reliever Abner Uribe received a one-game suspension and fine for inappropriate actions toward the St. Louis dugout.
cards.body:
Milwaukee Brewers reliever Abner Uribe has been suspended for one game and fined for inappropriate conduct directed at the St. Louis Cardinals dugout during their recent matchup. MLB announced the discipline Friday following a review of the incident.

The league office did not specify the amount of the fine accompanying the suspension.

cards.headline: French Open player retires after tripping on ad board
cards.teaser: Zeynep Sonmez retired from her doubles match after tripping over a courtside advertising board while chasing a ball.
cards.body:
Zeynep Sönmez was forced to retire from her doubles match at the French Open on Friday after tripping over a courtside advertising board. The incident happened while she was chasing down a ball during play at Roland Garros.

The fall led to her withdrawal from the match.

cards.headline: Luka Doncic invests in Rome basketball team
cards.teaser: Luka Doncic is partnering with former Mavericks executive Donnie Nelson to bring professional basketball to Rome.
cards.body:
Luka Dončić is partnering with Donnie Nelson, a former Dallas Mavericks executive, to establish a basketball team in Rome. The two previously worked together during Nelson's tenure with the Mavericks before he departed the organization.

The Rome-based franchise has submitted a bid to join the NBA Europe league, which is currently in development. This venture marks a new opportunity for both Dončić and Nelson as they work to build a basketball presence in Italy's capital.

hero.headline: Judge Orders Trump Name Removed From Kennedy Center, Halts Two-Year Renovation Closure
hero.body:
A federal judge has ruled that adding President Donald Trump's name to the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts violated federal law and ordered the removal of his name from the Washington DC venue within two weeks.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper determined that the Kennedy Center's board of trustees acted illegally when it voted to rename the arts complex. The judge stated in his ruling that the center "cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so."

The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Democratic representative from Ohio. Beatty challenged the board's authority to rename the federally designated venue without congressional approval. The Kennedy Center was originally established by Congress as the national cultural center and named in honor of President John F. Kennedy.

The judge's decision addressed a core legal question: whether the board of trustees had the power to make such a significant change to a federal institution on its own authority. Cooper's ruling concluded that they did not.

Cooper ordered Kennedy Center officials to comply with the name removal within 14 days of the ruling. The directive requires the removal of all physical signage bearing Trump's name and the elimination of any references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials.

The ruling also halted a planned two-year closure of the Kennedy Center for renovation work that had been announced alongside the name change decision. This closure would have suspended the venue's regular programming schedule during the renovation period. The court's order prevents this extensive shutdown, at least for now, though the judge did not make a permanent determination about future renovation plans.

The decision represents a significant legal setback for the renaming effort. It prevents not only the name change but also the lengthy operational disruption that had been scheduled to begin in the coming months. The renovation plans tied to the closure will require revision following the court order.

The Kennedy Center has not yet issued a public statement regarding whether it will appeal the judge's decision. The venue continues its regular programming schedule while the legal situation remains in flux.

The case reflects broader legal tensions about presidential authority and the proper role of institutional boards when managing federally designated properties. By requiring congressional approval for any renaming, the judge reinforced existing legal protections for federally established monuments and cultural institutions. The decision ensures that significant changes to such institutions require action from the legislative branch rather than unilateral decisions by boards of trustees.

cards.headline: Over Half of Great American State Fair Performers Drop Out Over Politics and Threats
cards.teaser: More than half of the scheduled performers at Great American State Fair concerts have withdrawn from the events.
cards.body:
Multiple artists have canceled their appearances at the US Freedom 250 concert series amid political concerns and reported threats. The wave of cancellations includes Martina McBride and Morris Day, according to reports from multiple news outlets.

The Freedom 250 concerts are linked to Trump and connected to celebrations of America's 250th anniversary. The series of events has encountered significant difficulties as artists continue to pull out. The cancellations have affected programming at state fair venues across the country.

cards.headline: UFC to Hold Mixed Martial Arts Event at White House for Trump's 80th Birthday
cards.teaser: President Trump invited UFC President Dana White to stage a mixed martial arts event on the South Lawn.
cards.body:
President Trump invited Dana White, president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, to organize a mixed martial arts event on the White House South Lawn. The event will celebrate both America's 250th anniversary and the president's 80th birthday.

The UFC showcase represents an expansion of event programming at the executive residence, marking both a national milestone and the president's birthday with the combat sports spectacle.

cards.headline: Backrooms Director Kane Parsons Discusses Film Adaptation of His Web Series
cards.teaser: The 20-year-old filmmaker behind the Backrooms web series brought his horror concept to theaters through A24.
cards.body:
Kane Parsons directed Backrooms, opening in theaters through A24 after previously creating a web series of the same name. The film earned substantial revenue from preview screenings and is projected to become one of A24's major releases.

Parsons, now 20 years old, discussed the filmmaking process and his concerns about the adaptation. He addressed topics including liminal spaces, working with studio executives, and potential sequels to the horror film.

cards.headline: Hannah Einbinder Criticizes Spencer Pratt's Los Angeles Mayoral Campaign
cards.teaser: The Hacks actress spoke out against Spencer Pratt's bid to become mayor of Los Angeles following her show's finale.
cards.body:
Hannah Einbinder publicly criticized Spencer Pratt's Los Angeles mayoral campaign following the series finale of Hacks. She emphasized the importance of resisting his candidacy and expressed concerns about wealthy Los Angeles residents who present themselves as Democrats or leftists while prioritizing their financial interests.

Einbinder shared her opposition to Pratt's run for mayor in the aftermath of her show's conclusion.

cards.headline: Taylor Swift Fans Speculate About Involvement in Toy Story 5 After Billboard Campaign
cards.teaser: New billboards for the Pixar sequel include references that fans interpret as hints about Taylor Swift's participation.
cards.body:
Disney and Pixar's new billboard campaign for Toy Story 5 has sparked fan theories about Taylor Swift's potential involvement. Observers have pointed to Easter eggs in the marketing materials, including the "TS" branding, as possible clues linking the pop star to the animated sequel.

Swifties have long hoped for an official announcement about her role in the film. The studio has yet to make any public statement regarding Swift's participation as production continues.

cards.headline: Hacks Production Filmed Series Finale at the Louvre in Paris
cards.teaser: The show's creators secured access to film at the famous art museum for the final episode.
cards.body:
The creators of Hacks, Lucia Aniello, Paul W. Downs and Jen Statsky, planned from the beginning to set the series finale in Paris. Their primary goal was filming at the Louvre, the art museum that houses the Mona Lisa.

The production obtained permission to shoot at the location for the show's concluding episode. A heist at the museum last year had reportedly made filming access more difficult to arrange.

hero.headline: Judge orders Trump's name removed from Kennedy Center, blocks closure
hero.body:
A federal judge ruled Friday that President Trump's name must be removed from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and blocked the venue from closing for planned renovations.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper determined that the Kennedy Center's board lacked the legal authority to rename the performing arts complex without congressional approval. In his 94-page ruling, Cooper wrote that Congress established the center's name through legislation, and "only Congress can change it."

"The Court has concluded that the Board overstepped its statutory bounds by unilaterally renaming the Kennedy Center after President Trump," Cooper stated in the decision.

The judge ordered the Trump administration to remove all physical signage bearing Trump's name and eliminate any references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials within 14 days. The ruling also halted the center's scheduled July closure, which was planned to allow for two years of renovations to proceed.

Cooper sided with Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio and ex officio board member, who challenged both the renaming and the closure plans. Beatty contested the decision to wind down programming during the renovation period.

The Kennedy Center, formally known as the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, opened in 1971 as the nation's cultural center and memorial to the 35th president. Congress created the center through legislation that designated it as a living memorial to Kennedy, establishing its name through statute.

Trump dismissed several Kennedy Center board members in February 2025 and appointed others of his choosing, enabling the board to approve the renaming. The renovation project represented a significant undertaking for the historic institution.

The ruling represents a setback for the Trump administration's efforts to reshape the Kennedy Center. Cooper determined that the board could not unilaterally change a name established by federal law, emphasizing that congressional action would be required for any name change.

The judge's decision takes effect immediately, meaning the Kennedy Center must continue its regular programming and operations. The venue cannot proceed with its planned closure or the renovation timeline until the legal question is resolved or Congress acts.

The ruling highlighted that while the president may pursue various initiatives, certain decisions affecting federally designated institutions require congressional authorization. Cooper's decision reinforces the principle that Congress maintains authority over the nation's property and oversight of how government institutions operate.

The Kennedy Center board has not yet commented on whether it will appeal the decision. The immediate effect of the ruling means the performing arts venue will remain open and operational while Trump's name is removed from all signage and materials.

cards.headline: Detention facility in New Jersey tests new DHS secretary
cards.teaser: A private immigration detention center has become the first major challenge for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
cards.body:
Delaney Hall, a private detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, has become a flashpoint in disputes over Trump administration immigration policies. Protesters have been arrested outside the 1,000-bed facility while detainees reportedly participate in a hunger strike.

Detainees have raised claims of inhumane living conditions and inadequate medical care at the facility. The center reopened last year and has been the scene of heightened tensions since then. New Jersey Governor Sherrill announced plans to create protected protest zones at the facility.

cards.headline: Bulgaria to end US military aircraft presence over visa dispute
cards.teaser: Bulgaria will end the stay of US military aircraft in Sofia after the Trump administration rejected visa-free travel for Bulgarian citizens.
cards.body:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced Friday that his country will end the US military aircraft presence in Sofia by the end of June. The decision comes after the Trump administration rejected Bulgaria's request for visa-free travel privileges for its citizens to the United States.

Radev indicated he had raised the visa issue with US officials. The military aircraft deployment had been part of broader defense cooperation between the two NATO allies.

cards.headline: Former Iowa schools chief sentenced to two years on immigration and gun charges
cards.teaser: Ian Roberts, who led Des Moines schools, pleaded guilty to falsely claiming citizenship and illegally possessing a firearm.
cards.body:
Ian Roberts, the former superintendent of Des Moines schools, was sentenced Friday to two years in prison. He pleaded guilty to federal charges of falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen and illegally possessing a firearm.

Roberts led one of Iowa's largest school districts, serving more than 30,000 students, until his arrest in 2023.

cards.headline: Former Attorney General Bondi addresses Epstein files missteps
cards.teaser: Pam Bondi appeared before officials to discuss mistakes in handling Epstein-related documents.
cards.body:
Former Attorney General Pam Bondi testified before Congress about errors in how the Justice Department handled files related to Jeffrey Epstein. During her closed-door testimony, Bondi acknowledged "redaction errors" in the documents while defending the department's overall management of the case.

Bondi characterized the Justice Department's approach as reflecting an "unprecedented commitment to transparency" in handling the Epstein files. Her testimony came approximately a month after she was removed from the position by President Donald Trump.

cards.headline: Jill Biden says husband's cancer diagnosis was shocking
cards.teaser: The former first lady discussed President Biden's prostate cancer in a new interview.
cards.body:
Former first lady Jill Biden discussed her husband's prostate cancer diagnosis in a recent CBS News interview with Rita Braver. She described the diagnosis as shocking and noted that the cancer had somehow gone undetected before it was eventually identified.

Former President Biden publicly revealed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May of the previous year, with a spokesperson confirming the news at that time.

cards.headline: UnitedHealthcare eliminates prior approval for most pediatric services
cards.teaser: The insurance giant will remove two-thirds of authorization requirements for members under 18 by year's end.
cards.body:
UnitedHealthcare announced it will drastically reduce prior authorization requirements for pediatric care. The company said it is removing two-thirds of authorization requirements for members under age 18 by the end of the year.

Physicians have criticized prior authorization processes as creating unnecessary barriers to timely and necessary medical care. The change represents a significant scaling back of requirements that doctors say delay treatment.
